findings.where: Nav bar, the logo at top left, and the hero drawing (the aqueduct mark drawn large)
findings.fault: The logo is shown in a white version the client doesn't hold. Mark's logo blue (#0070C0) and grey (#404040) appear nowhere on the page. The palette neither gives them a job nor declares them logo-only. The large mark in the hero also has things added to it: an amber hatch in the third bay, centre lines and dimension lines.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose blue wordmark is the one asset the brand sheet says stays. The founder too, because the house rules say a logo is never recoloured or changed without the client's yes. Mark would see his identity replaced by a drawing he hasn't approved.

findings.where: Hero, the line under the name ('LONGITUDINAL SECTION A–A • SCALE NTS'), the circled 'A', the 'NTS', 'EQ' and '±0.00' labels on the drawing, and the 'DRAWING MMM-GA-001 / SCALE NTS' cells in the nav
findings.fault: Drafting labels sit next to Mark's role and read as part of who he is. A visitor reads 'Infrastructure advisor, longitudinal section A–A, scale NTS', which means nothing to them. At phone width the line also wraps, leaving a lone bullet at the end of a line.
findings.who_objects: A senior development-bank official deciding whether to trust a legal advisor. The unexplained engineering codes slow the five-second read of who this is. They can also make the site look like a design exercise rather than a lawyer's practice.

findings.where: Nav bar title block, the 'DRAWING MMM-GA-001' and 'SCALE NTS' cells (top right at desktop, next to the logo at phone)
findings.fault: These two static cells sit in the same row of divided cells as Profile, Articles, Blog and Contact, in the same spaced capitals. They look like two more nav items, but clicking them does nothing.
findings.who_objects: A visitor scanning the nav for Contact or Profile. They may try the drawing number expecting a page, and the nav reads as six choices when there are four.

findings.where: Hero, the contact route ('Write to Mark' button and the Contact nav item) and the nav title block
findings.fault: The only contact is a mailto button that hides the email address. Mark's address is never shown in full as link text. The direction card says the title block should carry the contact, but it carries a drawing number and scale instead.
findings.who_objects: An official whose mail client doesn't open from mailto links, or who wants to copy the address into a procurement shortlist. They can't see where to write.

findings.where: Hero, the amber hatch in the third arch and the amber 'Write to Mark' button; the palette swatch 'Sodium amber — daylight in the drawing, and the one action'
findings.fault: The colour that marks the one action is also used as decoration in the drawing. The amber bay sits directly above the button, so the two compete, and the action colour no longer means only 'act here'.
findings.who_objects: The visitor, whose eye is drawn to the amber hatch in the picture before the button. Angélique, who is told amber is both decoration and the button. She can't tell which new uses would be right.

findings.where: Hero and the whole tile: no photograph of Mark, and no place given to one
findings.fault: Mark is never seen. This direction gives the layout round no place for his face on the blueprint sheet. The brief's client value 'the man himself' and the first-visit rule for a solo practice both ask for a real photo.
findings.who_objects: The visiting official, who wants to see the named person they would hire. Mark, who chose MacGeorge and his own site as references for showing himself.

findings.where: Article specimen ('An article page'), the body text and pull quote
findings.fault: The article is set as light text on mid-blue, with the full blueprint grid running through every line of prose. That is fine for a short specimen, but tiring and noisy for a full article. The brief's article pages are in Read mode.
findings.who_objects: An official reading a long piece on PPP law. The grid lines crossing the text and the reversed colours make a long read harder than it needs to be.

findings.where: Type pair note and the article specimen beneath it
findings.fault: The specimen breaks the type rules the tile states. The note says headings are ExtraBold capitals, but the article title is mixed case. The note says mono is for dates, but the article's date is in the text face, while the lecture row's date is in mono.
findings.who_objects: Angélique and the layout round. Faced with the stated rule and the example disagreeing, they don't know which to follow when adding a post.

findings.where: Hero copy, 'with over 40 years of international infrastructure experience'
findings.fault: The strongest line rests on a count of years rather than checkable work. The 'Lead Lawyer in the World Bank's PPP Group' fact next to it does that job better.
findings.who_objects: A procurement-minded official, who weighs named bodies, roles and regions over size claims. The brief's own 'no boasts' value also objects.

findings.where: Hero drawing, the thin S-curve rising from the ground line at the far right
findings.fault: A stray curve leaves the ground line and stops in mid-air. It isn't labelled as terrain or as part of the structure.
findings.who_objects: An infrastructure-literate visitor, who reads it as an unfinished or mistaken line in a drawing that otherwise claims to be measured and exact.

findings.fault: The earth-hatch and poche samples run flush against the panel's edges. The dimension line below them becomes an empty closed box, which looks broken and like an empty input field.
findings.who_objects: Mark or the founder reviewing the tile on a phone. The texture looks unfinished just where it is meant to show the look.

findings.where: Desktop, lower half: the article specimen column beside the motion sketch panel
findings.fault: The left column ends about 300 px before the motion panel on the right. That leaves a large empty block at the bottom left of the sheet, so the page ends lopsided.
findings.who_objects: A visitor reaching the end of the page, who sees an unbalanced sheet. That undercuts the precise, engineered impression the direction is going for.
